subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
This is the sixth and final unit of Year 7, and it brings together many of the ideas you have met all year: breaking a problem into steps, writing text-based code, using inputs and outputs, and testing your work. Here you focus on two powerful computational-thinking tools that professional programmers use every single day: sequencing and pattern recognition.

Sequencing means putting instructions in the correct order. A computer does exactly what you tell it, in the exact order you tell it. If you swap two steps around, the result changes — sometimes in a small way, sometimes completely. When you program a light sequence, the order of your instructions is the difference between a smooth, clear animation and a confusing flicker.

Pattern recognition means looking for things that repeat or that are similar, and then using what you notice to solve a problem faster. When you see the same block of code appearing again and again, that is a pattern — and it tells you that a loop could do the same job in far fewer lines. When you see that MakeCode blocks and MicroPython text use similar words, that pattern helps you translate between them. Spotting patterns is what turns a slow, copy-and-paste programmer into a fast, confident one.

concepts.title: Sequencing — Order Is Everything
concepts.example: What the simulator does: the digit 1 scrolls across the LEDs from right to left, then the device waits one second, then 2 scrolls, waits one second, then 3 scrolls. Now imagine you accidentally put the scroll(3) line first. The output would be 3, 2, 1 — the same instructions, but a completely different message, all because the sequence changed. This is a pattern you will see everywhere: same instructions, wrong order, wrong result.

concepts.title: The LED Display and Single Lights
concepts.explanation:
The front of the micro:bit is a 5 by 5 grid of 25 red LEDs. You can think of it like a tiny piece of squared paper where each square is a light. To talk about one particular light, you give its column number (x) and its row number (y). Both start counting from 0, not 1, and the top-left light is at position (0, 0).

x is the column: 0 is the far left, 4 is the far right.

y is the row: 0 is the top, 4 is the bottom.

So the very centre light is at x = 2, y = 2. The bottom-right light is at x = 4, y = 4.

The command display.set_pixel(x, y, brightness) turns one light on or off. Brightness is a number from 0 (off) to 9 (fully on). This program lights up only the centre LED at full brightness:

What the simulator does: a single light glows brightly in the exact middle of the grid; the other 24 stay dark. To light the top-left LED instead, you would change the coordinates to (0, 0): the line becomes display.set_pixel(0, 0, 9). To light the bottom-right LED, you would use display.set_pixel(4, 4, 9). Try predicting where the light will appear before you run it — that habit of predicting first is how good programmers check their own thinking.

In MicroPython each individual LED can be switched fully on with the number 9 or fully off with 0.
concepts.example: The numbers 1 to 8 in between give dimmer levels of red light, so 4 is roughly half brightness.

concepts.title: Showing Built
concepts.explanation:
Turning on lights one at a time works, but the micro:bit also comes with many ready-made pictures called images. You show one with display.show(). This program displays a heart:

What the simulator does: the LEDs light up in the shape of a heart and stay on. Notice the capital letters: Image and HEART must both be capitalised exactly, or the program will not run. There are many built-in images you can use in the same way, for example:

Image.HAPPY and Image.SAD — a smiling face and a frowning face

Image.HEART and Image.HEART_SMALL — a big and a small heart

Image.SQUARE and Image.SQUARE_SMALL — a large and a small square

Image.DIAMOND, Image.DIAMOND_SMALL, Image.TRIANGLE and Image.CHESSBOARD

Image.ARROW_N, Image.ARROW_E, and the other compass-direction arrows
concepts.example: This is a good moment to notice a pattern. When you moved from block-based MakeCode to text-based MicroPython, the block that shows a heart and the line display.show(Image.HEART) both contain the same key words: show and heart. Spotting that similarity helps you translate what you already know into new code. Pattern recognition is not only about pictures — it is also about noticing that two different tools use the same ideas.

concepts.title: Building Your Own Light Patterns
concepts.explanation:
The real power comes when you design your own patterns. You do this by describing all 25 lights at once using the Image() command with a text string. Inside the quotation marks you write five groups of five digits, one group for each row, separated by colons. Each digit sets the brightness of one LED, from 0 (off) to 9 (full).

The trick — and the pattern to recognise — is that the digits are laid out in the same 5 by 5 shape as the real display. If you write the digits neatly, the string is a picture of the lights. Here is a program that lights up only the left-hand column:

Reading the string: each row is 90000 — the first light (far left) is 9 (on) and the other four are 0 (off). Stacked over five rows, that draws a vertical line of five lights down the left edge. What the simulator does: a bright vertical line glows down the far-left column; the rest of the grid is dark. To move that line to the middle, you shift the 9 into the middle position of each row: Image("00900:00900:00900:00900:00900"). To move it to the right-hand column, put the 9 last in each row: Image("00009:00009:00009:00009:00009").

You can draw anything this way. Here is a full border square, exactly the same as the built-in Image.SQUARE, so you can see how the digits map to the picture:
concepts.example: What the simulator does: the outer edge of the grid lights up as a hollow square, with the centre nine lights left dark. (In the code above the string is split over several lines only to make the square easy to see; MicroPython joins the pieces back into one string.)

concepts.title: Controlling Brightness
concepts.explanation:
So far you have used only 0 and 9 — fully off or fully on. But the numbers 1 to 8 give you every level in between, from very dim to nearly full. This lets you make an image fade in or fade out, which is a lovely effect for an alarm because a pulsing light naturally draws the eye.

This program shows a plus sign (+) three times: first dim, then bright, then off. It uses the same shape each time and only changes the brightness digits, which is itself a clear pattern.

from microbit import * display.show(Image("00400:00400:44444:00400:00400")) # dim plus sleep(500) display.show(Image("00900:00900:99999:00900:00900")) # bright plus sleep(500) display.show(Image("00000:00000:00000:00000:00000")) # all off
concepts.example: What the simulator does: a faint plus sign appears (brightness 4), holds for half a second, then jumps to a strong bright plus (brightness 9) for half a second, then the screen clears. The last all-zero image is important: it is how you deliberately clear the display at the end of a sequence, so no lights are left glowing.

concepts.title: Making the Lights Move — A Light Sequence
concepts.example: What the simulator does: a vertical line glows on the far left for half a second, switches off, and a vertical line glows on the far right for half a second, then the screen clears. Because the two images appear quickly one after another, your brain reads it as a line moving across the display. The sleep(500) between them is essential — without a pause the images would swap far too fast to see.

concepts.title: Extending the Sequence
concepts.explanation:
Once you can show two images, adding a third, fourth or fifth is easy — you simply keep following the same pattern. To make the line sweep smoothly from left to right, you add a middle image between the left and right ones:

from microbit import * display.show(Image("90000:90000:90000:90000:90000")) # left sleep(500) display.show(Image("00900:00900:00900:00900:00900")) # middle sleep(500) display.show(Image("00009:00009:00009:00009:00009")) # right sleep(500) display.clear()
concepts.example: What the simulator does: the glowing line now appears on the left, then the middle, then the right, each for half a second, before clearing — a smooth sweep across the whole display. Look carefully at the code and you will see the pattern: every step is exactly 'display.show(...)' followed by 'sleep(500)'. Only the picture inside the brackets changes. Recognising this repeated shape is the key that unlocks the next, more powerful idea: loops.

concepts.title: Iteration — Using Loops to Capture a Pattern
concepts.explanation:
Look again at the last program. The line 'display.show(...)' followed by 'sleep(500)' appears three times. Copying and pasting works, but imagine a sequence with fifty images — you would be copying for a long time, and one small typo would be hard to find. This is where pattern recognition and iteration (looping) work together. When you notice that something repeats, you can put it inside a loop and let the micro:bit do the repeating for you.

A for loop repeats its indented lines once for each item in a list. Here we store the three images in a list called frames, then loop through them. The indented lines run once per frame:

from microbit import * frames = [ Image("90000:90000:90000:90000:90000"), # left Image("00900:00900:00900:00900:00900"), # middle Image("00009:00009:00009:00009:00009"), # right ] for frame in frames: display.show(frame) sleep(500) display.clear()

What the simulator does: exactly the same sweep as before — left, middle, right, then clear — but written in far fewer lines. The word frame is a temporary name that stands for each image in turn: the first time round the loop it is the left image, the second time the middle, the third time the right. The indentation (the spaces at the start of the two loop lines) tells MicroPython which lines belong inside the loop. This is the same indentation rule you use with IF statements.

A real alarm should keep flashing until someone notices it, not stop after one sweep. For that you use a while loop. The line while True: means 'keep repeating the indented lines forever'. Combining the two kinds of loop, this program sweeps the light across the display again and again, without stopping:

from microbit import * frames = [ Image("90000:90000:90000:90000:90000"), Image("00900:00900:00900:00900:00900"), Image("00009:00009:00009:00009:00009"), ] while True: for frame in frames: display.show(frame) sleep(500)

What the simulator does: the line sweeps left-to-right, then instantly starts again from the left, over and over, for as long as the program runs. There is one more shortcut worth knowing: display.show() can animate a whole list for you if you give it a delay. The single line display.show(frames, delay=500, loop=True) does the same endless sweep. Fewer lines, same result — that is the reward for spotting the pattern.

A loop that repeats a fixed number of times (like once per image in a list) is called a 'for' loop.

A loop that repeats while a condition stays true is called a 'while' loop.
concepts.example: 'while True:' never becomes false on its own, so it runs forever — perfect for an alarm that must keep flashing.

concepts.example: What the simulator does: the happy face shows while button A is not pressed, and the sad face shows while it is pressed — the reverse of what you might first expect. The word not flips True into False and False into True.

concepts.title: Sub
concepts.explanation:
A sub-routine is a mini-program inside your program. You write it once, give it a name, and then run it whenever you like just by using its name. In MicroPython you create a sub-routine with the word def (short for 'define'). Sub-routines make your code shorter, easier to read, and easier to test, because each one does a single, clearly named job.

Here we put the whole flashing light sequence into a sub-routine called light_sequence. Nothing inside it runs until we 'call' it by writing its name followed by brackets:

from microbit import * def light_sequence(): display.show(Image("90000:90000:90000:90000:90000")) sleep(300) display.show(Image("00900:00900:00900:00900:00900")) sleep(300) display.show(Image("00009:00009:00009:00009:00009")) sleep(300) display.clear() light_sequence() # run the sub-routine once
concepts.example: What the simulator does: the sweep left, middle, right plays once and clears — the same as before. The difference is in how the code is organised. The recipe now has a name, so the main part of your program can stay clean and simple: 'when the alarm should go off, run light_sequence()'. This matches how the textbook draws a flowchart with a sub-routine box: the box just says 'Light sequence', and the details live in their own separate flowchart.

concepts.title: Choosing the Input — Button, Shake or Sound
concepts.explanation:
For the visual alarm, the buzzer needs to start the light sequence. The micro:bit gives you three sensible inputs to represent that buzzer, and you can test all three in the simulator.

A button: button_a.is_pressed() — simple and reliable, but someone has to press it by hand.

A shake: accelerometer.was_gesture("shake") — becomes True when the device is shaken.

The sound sensor (microphone): microphone.sound_level() — returns a loudness value from 0 to 255, so a loud buzzer or clap can trigger the alarm on its own.

The sound sensor is the best match for our scenario, because it can react to the buzzer automatically without anyone touching the device. This program checks the microphone forever, and runs the light sequence whenever the sound is loud (above the halfway value of 128):

from microbit import * def light_sequence(): for i in range(3): display.show(Image("99999:99999:99999:99999:99999")) sleep(300) display.clear() sleep(300) while True: if microphone.sound_level() > 128: light_sequence() else: display.clear()
concepts.example: What the simulator does: the display stays dark while it is quiet. In the simulator, drag the sound-level slider up past the middle (or use your microphone if the site asks permission), and the whole grid flashes on and off three times — a clear, hard-to-miss alarm — before going quiet again. The sound sensor and microphone are features of the micro:bit version 2, and the online simulator fully supports them.

concepts.title: Prototyping — Building to Learn
concepts.explanation:
A prototype is a first working model of a product, built to test an idea before the final version is made. Software developers almost never write the finished program in one go. Instead they build a rough version, try it out, gather user feedback, fix the problems, and improve it. Releasing software that is full of bugs gives a bad impression and people stop using it, so prototyping and testing come first.

There are two common styles of prototyping, and you should know the difference:

Evolutionary prototyping: you build a full version, get feedback, improve it, and repeat. The prototype gradually 'evolves' into the finished product. Example: a complete game that is tested and refined again and again.

Throwaway prototyping: you build one small part, test just that part, learn from it, and then throw it away before building the real thing. Example: testing a single level of a game to check an idea, then discarding it.
concepts.example: For your visual alarm you will use a bit of both: you might build a quick throwaway test of just the flashing pattern to see if it catches the eye, then switch to evolutionary prototyping to add the sound sensor and keep improving the whole thing. A project plan guides all of this. It breaks the big problem into smaller questions — which input will start the alarm? what will the sequence look like? what happens when the alarm is off? — and answers each one before any final code is written.

concepts.title: Test Plans — Proving It Works
concepts.explanation:
How do you know your program really works, and not just that it worked the one time you tried it? You use a test plan: a table that lists each thing to test, the data you will enter, the result you expect, and a column to record whether the test passed or failed. Writing the test plan before you test forces you to be clear about what 'working correctly' actually means.

Here is an example test plan for a sound-activated alarm. You would run each test in the simulator and fill in the final column:

Notice test 3: it checks that the alarm does not go off when it should not. Good testing checks both that the right thing happens and that the wrong thing does not. If a test fails, you have found a bug — and finding it in testing, before anyone relies on your alarm, is exactly the point.

Test — Data entered · Expected outcome · Pass / Fail

1 — Loud sound (slider high) · Light sequence flashes 3 times · ...

2 — Sequence order · All-on, off, on, off, on, off in order · ...

3 — Quiet (slider low) · Display stays clear, no flashing · ...
concepts.example: 4 — After alarm finishes · Display returns to clear, ready for next sound · ...

concepts.title: Debugging with Pattern Recognition
concepts.explanation:
Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors. Pattern recognition is your best debugging tool. When a program does not behave as expected, compare it — line by line — against your flowchart or your grid drawings, and look for the place where the pattern breaks. If your sequence should be square, small square, chessboard, but the small square never appears, the broken line is easy to spot once you line the code up against the plan.

When there is a typing error in the code itself, the micro:bit shows a sad face and then scrolls a message telling you the line where the problem is. When that happens, work through this checklist — these are the most common MicroPython mistakes:

Does the program start with from microbit import * ?

Are all brackets ( ) and quotation marks " " opened and closed?

Is there a colon at the end of every if, else, for, while and def line?

Are the capital letters correct, for example Image.HEART and Image.HAPPY?

Is the indentation correct — are the lines inside a loop or if statement pushed in by spaces?

In an Image string, does each row have exactly five digits and a colon between rows?

Are all the command words spelled correctly, for example display and sleep?
concepts.example: One famous trap from this unit is the image name Image.SQUARE_SMALL. It is very easy to type SQUAR_SMALL by mistake, missing the E. That single missing letter makes the whole program crash, because MicroPython does not recognise the misspelled name. Careful spelling is not fussiness — to a computer, SQUARE_SMALL and SQUAR_SMALL are two completely different words.

methods.title: How to work with controlling brightness
methods.example: What the simulator does: a faint plus sign appears (brightness 4), holds for half a second, then jumps to a strong bright plus (brightness 9) for half a second, then the screen clears. The last all-zero image is important: it is how you deliberately clear the…

methods.title: How to work with making the lights move — a light sequence
methods.example: What the simulator does: a vertical line glows on the far left for half a second, switches off, and a vertical line glows on the far right for half a second, then the screen clears. Because the two images appear quickly one after another, your brain reads it…

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Flashing a real micro:bit is optional. Everything in this unit can be completed in the simulator. The microphone and sound sensor are micro:bit version 2 features, and the online simulator supports them. If the site asks to use your computer's microphone, you can allow it, or simply use the sound slider instead.

rules.title: the 5 by 5 grid
rules.text: The display is 25 LEDs in 5 columns (x = 0 to 4) and 5 rows (y = 0 to 4). The top-left LED is (0, 0). The centre is (2, 2). The bottom-right is (4, 4).

rules.title: brightness
rules.text: 0 means off and 9 means fully on. The numbers 1 to 8 are dimmer levels in between. Changing only the brightness digits lets an image fade in or out.

rules.title: time is in milliseconds
rules.text: There are 1000 milliseconds in one second, so sleep(1000) waits one second. Half a second is sleep(500). A pause is essential so each image can be seen.

rules.title: sequence and patterns
rules.text: The order of your lines is the order the lights display in. Wrong order means wrong message. If you see the same lines repeating, a loop can replace them. That is pattern recognition at work.

rules.title: debugging checklist
rules.text: First line present? Colons on if/for/while/def? Capitals and spelling correct? Brackets and quotes closed? Indentation consistent? Each Image row exactly 5 digits?

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Every MicroPython program in this unit begins with the same first line: from microbit import * This line imports everything you need to control the micro:bit's lights, buttons and sensors. The star symbol * here means 'everything'. Without this line, none of the micro:bit commands will work.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why the order of instructions matters in a light sequence. Give an example of what could go wrong.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The computer runs instructions strictly top to bottom, so the order decides the output. Example: if you show the 'right column' image before the 'left column' image, the light appears to move right-to-left instead of left-to-right — a different message.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between display.show() and display.scroll()?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: display.show() shows an image (or holds a single character) on the LEDs; display.scroll() slides text or numbers across the display from right to left.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between a for loop and a while loop.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A for loop repeats a fixed number of times (for example once per item in a list). A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true; while True: repeats forever.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the purpose of a sleep() command between two images in a sequence?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: sleep() pauses the program so each image is visible long enough for the eye to see before the next one replaces it. Without it, images swap too fast to notice.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe the difference between evolutionary and throwaway prototyping.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Evolutionary prototyping builds a full version, gathers feedback and improves it repeatedly until it becomes the final product. Throwaway prototyping builds a small part to test one idea, then discards it before building the real thing.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is a test plan useful? What are its main columns?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A test plan proves a program works as expected and helps find bugs before release. Its main columns are the test description, the data entered, the expected outcome, and the pass/fail result.
